tools.why: Turns one Claude Code session into a game studio: 49 agents from creative director to QA tester, 72 workflow skills, gates and templates. Its lightest mode goes from a one-page brief to a running game.

install.label: Clone it as your new project
install.cmd:
git clone https://github.com/Donchitos/Claude-Code-Game-Studios.git my-game
cd my-game
claude

caveats: Built for Godot, Unity and Unreal projects; this showcase uses its workflow with no engine (a plain web page), which is a departure.
Its hooks need Bash, Python 3 and ideally jq; one hook checks GitHub for updates (it can be turned off in /settings).
The heavier rigor levels write many documents before code; the README itself measures that the lightest level made the better game.

tools.why: Meng To's skills for playable three.js games: an isometric action-RPG loop built in vertical slices, camera, enemy AI, combat timing, readable VFX, audio cues, mobile controls and real-browser testing.

install.label: Copy the skill folders you need into your project
install.cmd:
git clone https://github.com/MengTo/Skills.git
mkdir -p .claude/skills
cp -r Skills/agent-skills/game-development/* .claude/skills/

caveats: The README's own setup notes say install instructions for Claude Code are still to come; copying the SKILL.md folders works.
Some skills assume generated or rigged 3D assets; this showcase uses procedural meshes only.

tools.why: The rigid-body physics engine inside Horizon Forbidden West and Death Stranding 2, built for many threads. Its official WebAssembly port brings the same bodies, constraints and buoyancy to the browser.

install.label: then
install.cmd:
import initJolt from 'jolt-physics';
const Jolt = await initJolt();

caveats: The browser build is the separate JoltPhysics.js repo by the same author; its API mirrors the C++ one, and objects you create with new must be freed with Jolt.destroy().

tools.why: Dan Greenheck's real-time mesh fracturing and slicing for three.js: Voronoi fractures concentrated around the impact, refracturing, plane slicing and separate materials for the broken insides.
caveats: It breaks meshes but doesn't move the pieces; pair it with a physics engine (this page uses Rapier).
Fracturing many fragments at once costs a frame or two; cap the count on phones.

tools.why: Volumetric fire, smoke and explosions for three.js, simulated as a sparse fluid on the GPU and ray-marched, with emitters, forces, colliders and a visual editor that exports effects.

install.label: or design an effect first in the hosted editor

caveats: WebGPU only: no WebGL fallback, and it's heavy on the GPU.
Very new (created September 2026, version 0.1.0); read the README's Limitations section.

tools.why: The industry-standard navmesh toolset behind the AI navigation in Unity, Unreal and Godot: Recast builds the mesh from level geometry, Detour finds paths, and DetourCrowd steers whole crowds around each other.
caveats: The browser build is a community port (isaac-mason/recast-navigation-js, MIT) of the C++ library.
The C++ repo has had no pushes since February 2026; it's mature rather than abandoned.

tools.why: A JavaScript port of mxgmn's WaveFunctionCollapse: learn the local patterns of a small sample, or the adjacency rules of a tile set, and grow whole maps that obey them.
caveats: Quiet since August 2023, and CommonJS only; load it through esm.sh in the browser.
Generation can hit a contradiction; retry with a new seed (this page shows the retries).

tools.why: A geometry library whose booleans always return solid, watertight meshes, fast enough to run live. Its WebAssembly build makes add-and-subtract level building possible in a browser.

install.label: then

caveats: Manifold objects live in WebAssembly memory; call delete() on the ones you no longer need.

tools.why: Arseny Kapoulkine's mesh optimisation library: simplification for LOD chains, vertex cache and overdraw ordering, and compression, with a JavaScript build and the gltfpack tool.

install.label: or optimise glTF files from the command line

caveats: The JavaScript build covers simplification, clustering, encoding and decoding; some C++ algorithms are not exposed.

tools.why: A zero-dependency JavaScript port of inkle's ink, the narrative scripting language behind 80 Days and Heaven's Vault, with a compiler that runs in the browser.

install.label: or a script tag (runtime and compiler)

caveats: A few API differences from the C# runtime and compiler, listed in the README.
Write the story in Inky (inkle's free editor) for a real project; this page compiles ink in the browser.
